auraIntro: Explorer, Sombrero Galaxy is famous for its bright white core and prominent dark dust lane.
overview: The Sombrero Galaxy (cataloged as M104 or NGC 4594) is an unbarred spiral galaxy in the constellation borders of Virgo and Corvus, roughly 31 million light-years from Earth.
formation: Formed approximately 13.2 billion years ago, its huge central bulge and prominent dust disk suggest complex early galactic mergers.
structure: Classified as an SAa spiral galaxy with a diameter of 50,000 light-years and a supermassive black hole exceeding 1 billion solar masses.
discoveryHistory: Discovered on May 11, 1781 by Pierre Méchain and independently noted by Charles Messier.
observationTips: Visible with binoculars under dark skies; 8-inch telescopes reveal the dark dust lane across the bright core.
funFacts: Possesses an unusually large globular cluster population estimated at nearly 2,000 clusters.
Houses a supermassive black hole with a mass 1 billion times that of our Sun at its center.

cards.title: Arrival: The Wide-Brimmed Cosmic Hat
cards.subtitle: Messier 104 Overview
cards.body: Welcome to the Sombrero Galaxy (M104), one of the most visually distinctive galaxies in the cosmos. Located 31 million light-years away on the border of Virgo and Corvus, M104 features a brilliant white nuclear bulge encircled by a prominent dark equatorial lane of interstellar dust, giving it the shape of a broad-brimmed Mexican hat.

cards.title: Discovery: Pierre Méchain & The Dust Lane
cards.subtitle: Catalogue History
cards.body: Discovered on May 11, 1781 by French astronomer Pierre Méchain, M104 was added to Messier's catalog posthumously by Camille Flammarion in 1921. Early 20th-century spectroscopic measurements by Vesto Slipher revealed its high radial velocity, providing early clues that spiral nebulae were expanding away from us.
bulletPoints: Pierre Méchain documented M104 in May 1781.
Vesto Slipher measured its high blueshift/redshift velocity in 1912.
Proved to be a distant extragalactic system outside the Milky Way.

cards.title: Cosmic Story: The 1 Billion Solar Mass Monster
cards.subtitle: Supermassive Core & Halo Clusters
cards.body: At the center of M104's brilliant stellar bulge lies a giant supermassive black hole with a mass exceeding 1 billion Suns—one of the most massive black holes detected in any nearby galaxy. Orbiting in the galaxy's vast halo are nearly 2,000 globular star clusters, roughly ten times the number surrounding the Milky Way.
bulletPoints: Central black hole mass measured at ~1,000,000,000 solar masses.
Halo contains ~2,000 ancient globular star clusters.
Chandra X-ray Observatory detects hot gas halo extending 60,000 light-years into space.

visualPlaceholder.title: Chandra X-Ray Emission Overlay
visualPlaceholder.caption: X-ray emission map showing hot diffuse gas extending far above M104's disk.

cards.title: Deep Insight: Webb Mid-Infrared Clumpy Dust Ring
cards.subtitle: Multi-Spectrum Space Observations
cards.body: NASA's James Webb Space Telescope imaged the Sombrero Galaxy in mid-infrared wavelengths using MIRI. Infrared light penetrates the dark dust lane, revealing an intricate clumpy ring structure containing cold gas and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) where active starbirth occurs.
bulletPoints: JWST MIRI mid-infrared optics penetrate optical dust opacity.
Reveals detailed clumpy dust ring structure in place of a smooth band.
Traces hydrocarbon chemistry and raw cold gas reservoirs.

visualPlaceholder.title: JWST MIRI Infrared Portrait
visualPlaceholder.caption: James Webb Space Telescope mid-infrared image revealing glowing dust structure inside M104's ring.

cards.title: Cosmic Curiosity: Hybrid Galaxy Evolution
cards.subtitle: Spiral Disk Inside Elliptical Bulge
cards.body: The Sombrero Galaxy presents a fascinating evolutionary riddle: it possesses both a massive, giant elliptical-like stellar bulge and a thin, gas-rich spiral disk. Astronomers hypothesize that M104 represents a rare hybrid galaxy formed when a gas-rich spiral was absorbed by a giant elliptical galaxy billions of years ago.
bulletPoints: Exhibits characteristics of both elliptical and spiral galaxy classes.
Enormous bulge component dominates total galaxy light and mass.
May represent a transitional evolutionary stage between spiral and elliptical forms.
